query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A short, sub-eutectic heat treatment following mild cold work will refine the lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure in the eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, thereby simultaneously increasing its strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure providing high ductility (~25%) but moderate strength (~944 MPa), where cold work alone (e.g., to >10–20% strain) increases strength at the expense of ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply mild cold work (approximately 10–20% deformation) to the as-cast alloy followed by a short post-processing heat treatment at 700–800°C for about 1 hour and then rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: Room temperature tensile testing and service conditions typical for structural applications; the treatment should be performed after light mechanical deformation without inducing excessive plastic strain.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined interlamellar structure with potentially reduced lamellar spacing and more coherent phase interfaces between the fcc and B2 regions.
generation.mechanism: The heat treatment facilitates partial recovery and recrystallization at the phase interfaces after mild cold work, refining the lamellar architecture. This improved microstructural configuration promotes more efficient dislocation slip and strain hardening across the fcc/B2 interfaces, thus reducing stress concentrations and enhancing both tensile strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the non-treated as-cast alloy and cold-rolled alloy that suffers a trade-off (e.g., strength increases above ~1200 MPa but ductility drops to ~10%), the treated alloy is expected to exhibit a simultaneous improvement in strength (targeting a significant increase relative to the as-cast state) while maintaining or even moderately improving ductility (relative to the degraded ductility observed after cold work alone).
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic HEA with ~944 MPa strength and ~25% ductility, and cold-rolled samples where strength improvements are accompanied by a drop in ductility (~10%).
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only within the processing window of mild plastic deformation (10–20% strain) and heat treatment temperatures of 700–800°C for approximately 1 hour; excessive deformation or deviations from these thermal parameters might instead promote grain coarsening or undesirable phase transformations that could negate the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by prior observations on lamellar refinement and interface coherence in eutectic HEAs, the exact quantitative improvements in strength and ductility and the optimal processing parameters remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy specimens. Subject one set to no further treatment, a second set to mild cold work (10–20% strain) only, and a third set to mild cold work followed by a post-processing heat treatment at 700–800°C for 1 hour with rapid quenching. Maintain identical sample dimensions and test conditions across groups.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (lamellar spacing and interface coherence via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-processed samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both strength (above the as-cast and cold-worked baseline) and ductility (i.e., ductility not reduced compared to the as-cast state) relative to both the untreated and cold-worked specimens, then the hypothesis that the short heat treatment refines the microstructure to overcome the strength–ductility trade-off would be falsified.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. decision.trend: Early work on the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA showed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with good as-cast strength (~944 MPa) and ductility (~25.6%). However, cold rolling to boost strength above 1200 MPa led to reduced ductility (~10%), illustrating the classic trade-off. Researchers found that multi-phase microstructures can enhance strength and ductility but require careful control of phase spacing and morphology. The remaining challenge is to refine the lamellae or phase architecture in a way that increases both strength and ductility without simply shifting the trade-off.
decision.unsolved: How to tailor the lamellar architecture or phase distribution in a eutectic HEA so that more efficient strain hardening and slip transfer are enabled, thereby enhancing both strength and ductility.
decision.lever: Implement a short post-processing heat treatment at 700–800°C for ~1 hour after light cold work (~10–20%) to partially refine and stabilize the interlamellar structure, followed by rapid quenching.
decision.why: Prior findings suggest that the as-cast lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 already balances strength and ductility, but cold deformation alone reduces ductility. A brief sub-eutectic anneal after mild cold work can refine lamellar spacing and promote beneficial interface structures, improving dislocation slip compatibility across phases. This approach is directly motivated by the observed relationship between lamellar refinement and mechanical performance in EHEAs, aiming to achieve higher strength without sacrificing ductility.
